title: Stoic in the world
hook: the two cities: your town and all humanity

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Handbook, where Epictetus says you kiss a mortal. Your line was mortal, and loved.

Your phone shows you a flood on another continent, a war, an election two oceans away, a famine far away. Then, in the same scroll, a post from your neighborhood group: someone's lost a dog, the library needs volunteers, the potholes on Elm Street. Two worlds, one screen, and a pull to care about all of it, with very little anyone can do about most of it. Seneca had an old idea for exactly this: two cities.
screen: `A FLOOD ON ANOTHER CONTINENT.` → `A LOST DOG ON ELM STREET.` → `TWO WORLDS, ONE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: First, the two cities. Seneca writes that each of us belongs to two commonwealths. One is huge and truly shared, by gods and humans alike, whose borders we measure by the path of the sun. The other is the one we happened to be born into: Athens, Carthage, or wherever. Some people serve both at once, he says; some only the larger, some only the smaller. Second, Marcus's version. As Antoninus, he writes, his city and country is Rome; as a human being, it is the world. The emperor of Rome, reminding himself privately that Rome wasn't the biggest thing he belonged to. Third, the old word. Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he came from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world. Kosmopolitēs. The Stoics took up the idea and gave it weight; Marcus calls every human being a fellow citizen. Fourth, the phone. The world city is too big to carry alone; nobody can fix the flood. But you can do one real thing for it: give, learn, speak up, treat a stranger online as a fellow citizen. And the small city is close enough to touch: the dog, the library, the pothole. The Stoic in the world doesn't drown in the big city or hide in the small one. They serve both, a little, on purpose. That turns helpless scrolling back into citizenship.
screen: `TWO COMMONWEALTHS, LARGE AND SMALL.` · `AS ANTONINUS, ROME; AS HUMAN, THE WORLD.` · `KOSMOPOLITĒS: CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.` · `ONE REAL THING FOR EACH CITY.` · then, large: `BOTH CITIES.`

segments.voice: Picture your small city first, your street, your town, and one face from it, a neighbor or a shopkeeper. Then let the view widen like a camera pulling back, to your country, the whole planet turning in the sun, and somewhere on it one stranger you'll never meet, living their ordinary day. Hold both faces, and let one small thing for each city come to mind.
Kosmopolitēs, citizen of the world, Diogenes the Cynic's old answer, taken up by the Stoics to mean belonging to all humanity. Today's word.
Your line: both cities. The street and the planet both count you as a citizen. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners think of themselves as citizens of both their local community and all humanity, and try to do something concrete for each.

original.note: Greek: citizen of the world, a word credited to Diogenes the Cynic.

trapdoor: what you thought: a citizen of the world is someone who travels a lot.
what it means: every human being is a fellow citizen; you belong to your town and to all humanity.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 6.63 credits Diogenes with kosmopolitēs; Seneca's On Leisure 4 has the two res publicae; Meditations 6.44 has Rome as Antoninus, the world as a human being.

chat.meaning: Seneca says we belong to two commonwealths, and Marcus calls every human a fellow citizen. You can't fix everything, but you can serve both, a little.

Kosmopolitēs.meaning: Greek for citizen of the world

Diogenes the Cynic.meaning: a Greek philosopher said to call himself a citizen of the world

Carthage.meaning: an ancient city in North Africa; Seneca's example of a birthplace

Antoninus.meaning: part of Marcus's own name as emperor
